synopsis: RIFT constructs future-position attention keys and values with one learned anticipation-token pass, then reuses that cache throughout action denoising. Its central distinction is between needing a future representation and needing iterative video generation to produce it. Cache interventions motivate the interface; a separately trained producer establishes rollout-free control performance. The reported policy achieves 98.8% LIBERO success at 247.9 ms per action chunk. All execution evidence is from simulation, and diagnostic future decodes do not establish physical robot performance. [e3, e5, e6, e10, e15]

problem.text: Existing comparisons between rollout-based WAMs and current-only policies change both the future representation available to the controller and the computation producing it. The paper asks whether meaningful future conditioning can remain at deployment while eliminating iterative video generation.

contributions.text: A paired closed-loop intervention protocol tests the controller's use of future-position attention caches through masking, value corruption, position reassignment, and fixed final-clean cache replay.

The authors distinguish consumption-side sufficiency from producer-side feasibility: replaying a rollout-derived clean cache can preserve behavior, but this alone does not establish that one pass can construct an effective cache.
RIFT supplies that producer using aligned anticipation tokens and auxiliary conditional flow matching, obtaining competitive simulated control success with substantially lower deployment latency.

inputs: Current observation o, including multi-camera imagery, and language instruction l. [e6, e9]
Learned anticipation tokens E at future spatiotemporal positions; aligned ground-truth future latent patches Y supply training supervision. [e6, e7]
outputs: A fixed future-position K/V cache at every video-stack layer and an action chunk with horizon H = 32. [e6]
Auxiliary future-flow predictions and a deterministic latent probe, excluded from policy-only deployment. [e7, e8]

steps.name: Establish whether the controller uses its future cache
steps.detail: Record per-layer future K/V during the original policy's generation. Replay action denoising with non-target inputs fixed. Value edits preserve recorded keys; final-clean replay substitutes both keys and values. Execute paired simulator episodes from the same initial state and policy seed.

steps.name: Construct aligned future states
steps.detail: Replace rollout tokens with learned E at their original future positions. Full alignment uses m = n(T_lat − 1), giving 196 tokens for LIBERO and 240 for RoboTwin. One video-stack pass over the current-frame tokens and E writes the complete per-layer cache.

steps.name: Preserve directional attention
steps.detail: Current-frame tokens attend only the observed frame. Anticipation tokens attend the current frame and one another. Video tokens cannot attend action tokens, making the cache action-independent conditional on observations and language.

steps.name: Generate and execute action chunks
steps.detail: The inherited action expert reads the same cache for all 10 action flow-matching steps and produces a 32-action chunk. Deployment performs one prefill per chunk. Closed-loop success evaluates simulator execution; decoded future images are separate diagnostics.

training.text: Each optimization step uses two forwards through the shared video expert. The first applies native video-flow supervision to a clean first frame and noised future latents, without anticipation tokens or action supervision. The second uses the deployment input [f0; E] for action and auxiliary future supervision.

Conditional flow matching trains a future-latent velocity head conditioned on final anticipation states S_phi. This shapes the producer without requiring direct regression to one observed future. The authors motivate it by the conditional-mean behavior of squared-error regression under multimodal futures.

Action loss updates the action expert, video expert, and anticipation tokens; future FM updates the producer and FM head. An RMS-normalized linear probe receives stopped-gradient states, so its MSE updates only the probe. After 70% of training, observation perturbation increases only for future-supervised rows; perturbed rows are excluded from action loss. Auxiliary weights decay from 1 to 0.2 over the final 30%.

inference.text: Policy-only inference retains the video-stack prefill, fixed future K/V, and action flow. It removes video denoising, VAE decoding, ground-truth futures, and both auxiliary heads. The latency measurement excludes the optional uncertainty monitor.

The anticipation cache is an action-independent conditional future representation. The described controller does not evaluate candidate action-conditioned video rollouts or optimize actions through a simulator at deployment.

equations.expression: C_phi(o,l) = {(K_E^(ell), V_E^(ell))}_{ell=1}^L = CachePrefill_phi([f0(o); E], o, l); a_hat_{1:H} = ActionDenoise(o,l; C_phi(o,l)).
equations.explanation: Equations (2)–(3) separate the cache producer from action generation. Phi includes the video expert and E; L is stack depth. C_phi has no action-flow index, so every denoising evaluation reads the same keys and values.

equations.expression: X_sigma = (1 − sigma)Y + sigma epsilon; v_sigma* = epsilon − Y; L_FM = E[w_vid(sigma) ||v_psi(X_sigma, sigma; S_phi) − v_sigma*||_2^2].
equations.explanation: Equations (4)–(5) interpolate clean future patches Y with Gaussian noise epsilon. The training-only head predicts the bridge velocity conditioned on anticipation states. Its gradients teach future information to the deployed producer.

equations.expression: L = L_vid + L_act + lambda_FM L_FM + lambda_probe L_probe.
equations.explanation: Equation (6) combines native video learning, deployment-matched action learning, and auxiliary supervision. The probe term cannot alter the controller because its input is detached.

Equation (1) measures intervention-induced end-effector drift over the common executed prefix, excluding reset pose. Recorded simulator positions are averaged within tasks and then across tasks. This measures deviation from Original, not distance to an optimal trajectory.

results.setting: Fast-WAM-Joint; 2,000 paired simulator trials across all 40 LIBERO tasks for each intervention.
results.metric: Task-macro EE-ADE in cm; task success rate
results.value: Masked future: 18.725 cm, 9.7% SR; spatial shuffle: 14.306 cm, 65.2% SR; temporal swap: 15.606 cm, 0.7% SR.
results.comparison: Original: 0 cm by definition and 98.4% SR.
results.interpretation: Reported execution changes support sensitivity to future content and position assignments. Similar spatial/temporal drift accompanies very different completion rates; EE-ADE is not interchangeable with task success.

results.setting: Final-clean K/V replay; 2,000 paired LIBERO trials per model. Intervals use task-cluster bootstrap.
results.metric: EE-ADE with 95% confidence interval; success rate
results.comparison: Both Original policies achieve 98.4% SR. IDM and LingBot-VA already consume fixed clean caches, making this intervention structurally N/A.
results.interpretation: A complete fixed cache nearly preserves these policies' behavior. The cache still originates from iterative generation, and this intervention does not isolate keys from values.

results.setting: One checkpoint per method; three evaluation seeds, each with 2,000 episodes across 40 tasks.
results.metric: Success rate, mean ± standard deviation across evaluation seeds
results.interpretation: RIFT has the highest reported mean, improving over current-only Fast-WAM by 2.0 percentage points. These deviations quantify evaluation variability, not uncertainty across independently trained models.

results.setting: One A800 GPU; each method's original denoising configuration; policy-only action-chunk latency.
results.comparison: Fast-WAM: 235.7 ms; PFD: 257.0 ms; Joint: 780.2 ms; IDM: 1081.2 ms; LingBot-VA: 2270.3 ms.
results.interpretation: Reported latency reductions versus rollout methods span 68.2–89.1%. This is an operational comparison under different native sampling configurations, not a comparison with equal denoising-step counts.

results.setting: No additional training; one rollout for each of 10,030 variants, environment/policy seed 42 and initial-state index 0.
results.interpretation: RIFT improves over IDM by approximately 9.7 percentage points and leads all seven perturbation categories. These are single-protocol point estimates, with no repeated-training uncertainty.

results.setting: 50 tasks; 100 trials per task in each clean/randomized setting; one checkpoint and single evaluation seed per method.
results.interpretation: RIFT has the highest observed aggregate rates, but its small margins over PFD lack reported uncertainty. These remain simulated bimanual execution results.

results.setting: LIBERO; identical one-pass deployment graph and 247.9 ms action-chunk cost.
results.metric: Success rate across three evaluation seeds
results.comparison: Approximately 0.4 percentage-point improvement for the full recipe.
results.interpretation: The improvement is small, and the full recipe includes its conditioning curriculum. This comparison supports the recipe but does not cleanly isolate the FM objective alone.

limitations.text: Evaluation is simulation-only. Physical deployment and transfer to non-WAM fusion architectures remain untested.

Shuffle and noise interventions are out of distribution. Their effects establish sensitivity at the cache interface, but should not be treated as a complete semantic account of future reasoning. The paper appropriately includes structured frozen-present and final-clean controls.

The introduction describes final-clean values replayed under original keys, whereas the detailed protocol and Table 3 specify replacement of both K and V. This report follows the detailed full-cache definition; the inconsistency prevents treating that result as an isolated value-only experiment.

The optional warning is not a calibrated failure probability. Appendix E reports that the mean CUSUM curve over 33 failed rollouts crosses threshold 210 steps before a common endpoint, which does not establish mean individual detection lead time despite stronger wording in Figure 7's caption. Both future estimators may agree on an incorrect future.

reproduction.text: Reproduction requires the inherited Wan2.2-5B video components and action expert, totaling approximately 6B parameters, exact future-position masks, latent patch alignment, and native flow-loss weighting. Reported settings include AdamW at 10^-4 learning rate, 0.01 weight decay, cosine annealing, gradient clipping at 1.0, and 20k LIBERO or 30k RoboTwin steps. RoboTwin training uses 2,500 clean and 25,000 randomized demonstrations.

The supplied configuration does not establish batch size, training accelerator count, detailed FM-head architecture, or checkpoint-selection rules. No code was inspected and no experiments were reproduced in this review.

A focused replication should first verify exact unedited replay and paired final-clean K/V replay. To test the producer mechanism, compare current-only, anticipation tokens without future supervision, L2, and FM using identical curricula and several training seeds; otherwise extra token capacity and curriculum remain alternative explanations.

reasoning.text: The WAM and efficient-inference classifications are supported. The exact Dual-system × IDM quadrant is less secure: RIFT retains Fast-WAM-Joint's video/action architecture but replaces joint rollout with an action-independent prefill followed by cache-conditioned action flow. This resembles a sequential future-to-action interface, yet the text does not explicitly establish a conventional generated-future inverse-dynamics model. Separate experts alone do not resolve the system boundary, and joint training alone would not prove One Model. Latent prediction is explicit; the supplied objective does not establish JEPA. The recorded snapshot is therefore preserved without endorsing every label.

discussionQuestions: Would an equally sized anticipation interface trained only through action loss retain the gains, separating future supervision from added representational capacity? [e6, e7, e13]
Does conditional FM outperform L2 when both use exactly the same perturbation curriculum and multiple training seeds? [e13]
How does an action-independent cache handle tasks whose plausible futures depend strongly on alternative action choices? [e6]
What are the optional monitor's episode-level false-alarm rate and detection lead-time distribution on held-out trajectories? [e14]

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author block, and arXiv version line
evidence.detail: The supplied title and all five authors match the catalog. The artifact identifies itself as arXiv:2608.11521v2, dated 13 August 2026.
The paper separates the future representation consumed by an action expert from iterative rollout that produces it, motivating explicit future conditioning without video generation.

Video cannot attend action tokens. Recorded caches support replay with fixed non-target inputs. Paired episodes share initial state and policy seed. EE-ADE uses simulator positions over the common prefix and task-macro averaging; shuffle and noise are acknowledged as out of distribution.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section 1 intervention paragraph; p. 4, Section 3.4; p. 10, Table 3, Fast-WAM-Joint rows
evidence.detail: Joint Original SR is 98.4%; masking, spatial shuffle, and temporal swap yield 9.7%, 65.2%, and 0.7%. Table 3 gives corresponding EE-ADEs of 18.725, 14.306, and 15.606 cm. Each estimate uses 2,000 paired trials across 40 tasks.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section 3.5; p. 10, Table 3 caption and Final clean K/V rows
evidence.detail: Full-cache replay fixes both K and V. Joint/Cosmos-2 SR is 97.9/98.2 versus 98.4/98.4 originally. Their EE-ADEs are 1.908 [1.579, 2.260] and 1.690 [0.260, 3.620] cm with task-bootstrap 95% intervals. Clean futures still come from rollout; IDM-style replay is structurally redundant.

RIFT preserves Fast-WAM-Joint's architecture and future-read interface. Aligned E tokens produce a complete cache in one prefill, with m = 196/240 for LIBERO/RoboTwin and H = 32. Directional attention makes the cache action-independent and reusable throughout action denoising.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 4.3, Eqs. (4)–(6); p. 10, Appendix A loss normalization, perturbation, and gradient routes
evidence.detail: Two shared-expert forwards provide native video supervision and deployment-matched action/future supervision. Conditional FM predicts epsilon minus Y along the stated bridge. Perturbed rows are excluded from action loss; perturbation reaches probability 0.3 and scale 0.06 latent standard deviations. Auxiliary weights decay from 1 to 0.2 after 70% of training.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 4.3 stopped-gradient linear probe; p. 10, Appendix A Diagnostic probe and Gradient routes
evidence.detail: The linear probe reads RMS-normalized detached anticipation states and minimizes elementwise future-latent MSE. Only probe parameters receive its gradients; the probe does not feed policy control.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 5.1 Implementation; p. 10, Appendix A Architecture and training configuration
evidence.detail: Matched LIBERO models share Wan2.2-5B, data, and a 20k-step budget. The action expert has width 1024, about 1B parameters and 6B total. Appendix A specifies camera concatenation, native flow scheduling, 10 action steps, guidance 1.0, optimizer settings, and 20k/30k training budgets.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 5.1 Benchmarks, Table 1, and Section 5.2 LIBERO
evidence.detail: Table 1 supplies all reported LIBERO success means, evaluation-seed deviations, and A800 chunk latencies. Three seeds evaluate one checkpoint with 2,000 trials each. Latencies use each method's original sampling configuration; RIFT excludes optional diagnostics.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Appendix D; p. 11, Table 5 caption and panel (a)
evidence.detail: The pinned OOD protocol evaluates 10,030 variants once without retraining, using seed 42 and initial-state index 0. Variant-micro SR is 49.73/68.06/71.36/81.07 for Fast-WAM/Joint/IDM/RIFT. RIFT leads all seven perturbation categories.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 5.1 RoboTwin setup; p. 7, Table 2
evidence.detail: The benchmark has 50 bimanual tasks and 100 trials per task per setting. The matched family trains on 2,500 clean and 25,000 randomized demonstrations. Single-seed aggregate clean/randomized rates are RIFT 92.9/92.6, PFD 92.5/92.1, Joint 91.0/91.1, and LingBot-VA 92.4/91.4.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Section 5.3 Anticipation-token supervision and token-count discussion; p. 11, Table 4
evidence.detail: Direct L2 achieves 98.37 ± 0.12 versus full FM 98.8 ± 0.17 at identical 247.9 ms deployment cost. The paper notes the small difference and inclusion of the conditioning curriculum. The textual token sweep identifies full alignment as best for both recipes.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 5.4 and Figure 7 caption; pp. 10–11, Appendix E, Eqs. (7)–(8)
evidence.detail: The optional monitor compares probe/FM mean disagreement with FM sample dispersion. Calibration uses 1,967 successes; 33 failures are excluded. Appendix E describes the average failed-rollout CUSUM crossing 210 steps before common endpoint 420, while the caption describes average alarm lead time. The statistic is not a failure probability and is excluded from policy latency.

evidence.location: PDF p. 11, Appendices F–G; pp. 13–14, Figures 8–9 captions
evidence.detail: The authors identify simulation-only evaluation and leave physical robots and non-WAM fusion backbones to future work. Future decodes are diagnostic; the trained probe and VAE decoding are outside deployed action generation.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section 1 final-clean paragraph; p. 3, Section 3.1; p. 4, Section 3.5; p. 10, Table 3 caption
evidence.detail: The introduction describes final clean values under original keys. The detailed method and uncertainty-table caption instead define final-clean replay as replacing both keys and values with a fixed complete cache.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section 2 World action models; p. 4, Section 4.2; p. 10, Appendix A architecture
evidence.detail: Related work distinguishes generated-video inverse dynamics from shared-attention joint denoising. RIFT retains the Joint architecture and its per-layer interface, with separate video and action experts, but changes deployment to one prefill followed by fixed-cache action denoising.
